title.en: Ancoallo: The Embalmed Brother Who Led the Chancas to War
title.zh: 安科阿約:率昌卡出征的兄弟乾屍

region.zh: 昌卡人的安達瓦伊利亞斯(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 26, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: In the province of Andahuaylas, thirty leagues west of Cuzco, there were two Sinchis named Uscovilca and Ancovilca, who coming on an expedition from near Huamanca had settled in the valley and formed a state. They were brothers. Uscovilca, the elder and principal, instituted a tribe called Hanan-chancas or upper Chancas; Ancovilca formed another called Hurin-chancas or lower Chancas. These chiefs, after death, were embalmed, and because they were feared for their cruelties in life, were kept by their people. The Hanan-chancas carried the statue of Uscovilca with them in their raids and wars; although they had other Sinchis, they always attributed their success to the statue of Uscovilca, which they called Ancoallo.
summary.zh: 庫斯科以西三十萊格的安達瓦伊利亞斯省,有兩位辛奇——烏斯科維爾卡與安科維爾卡——自瓦曼卡一帶遷來,在谷中建邦。二人為兄弟:兄長烏斯科維爾卡立「哈南昌卡」(上昌卡)部,安科維爾卡立「烏林昌卡」(下昌卡)部。二酋死後,因其生前兇名赫赫,遺體被製成木乃伊,由族人奉養。哈南昌卡人出征劫掠,必抬烏斯科維爾卡的神像隨行;雖另有辛奇統兵,卻總把勝利歸功於那尊名為「安科阿約」的烏斯科維爾卡神像。

sensitivity.note: The Chanca war-god as ancestor mummy; the mirror image of the Inca guauqui system on the enemy side.

passages.text: In this province there were two Sinchis, named Uscovilca and Ancovilca who, coming on an expedition from near Huamanca with some companies, had settled in the valley of Andahuaylas, and had there formed a state. They were brothers. Uscovilca being the elder and principal one, instituted a tribe which he called Hanan-chancas or upper Chancas. Ancovilca formed another tribe called Hurin-chancas or lower Chancas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: These chiefs, after death, were embalmed, and because they were feared for their cruelties in life, were kept by their people. The Hanan-chancas carried the statue of Uscovilca with them, in their raids and wars. Although they had other Sinchis, they always attributed their success to the statue of Uscovilca, which they called Ancoallo.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: 'I Will Not Abandon the House of the Sun': Cusi Rebukes His Father
title.zh: 「我決不捨棄太陽之屋」:庫西斥父逃亡

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 26, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The news of the Chanca advance spread terror among the orejones of Cuzco, for they doubted the powers of Inca Viracocha, who was now very old and weak. Viracocha called a Council of his sons and captains Apu Mayta and Vicaquirau. These captains said to him: 'After careful consideration it appears to us that, as you are old and infirm, it will not be well that you should attempt so great a business, dangerous and with victory doubtful. The wisest counsel is that you should leave Cuzco, and proceed to the place of Chita, and thence to Caquia Xaquixahuana, which is a strong fort, whence you may treat for an agreement with the Chancas.' But when Cusi Inca Yupanqui found that his father was determined to leave Cuzco, they say that he thus addressed him: 'How father can it fit into your heart to accept such infamous advice as to leave Cuzco, city of the Sun and of Viracocha, whose name you have taken, whose promise you hold that you shall be a great lord, you and your descendants.' Though a boy, he said this with the animated daring of a man high in honour. The father answered that he was a boy and that he spoke like one, in talking without consideration, and that such words were of no value. Inca Yupanqui replied that he would remain where they would be remembered, that he would not leave Cuzco nor abandon the House of the Sun. So Viracocha left Cuzco and went to Chita; his son Inca Yupanqui remained at Cuzco, resolved to defend the city or die in its defence. Seven chiefs remained with him.
summary.zh: 昌卡進逼的消息令庫斯科的耳垂貴胄膽寒——老王維拉科查年老體衰,威望堪憂。維拉科查召集諸子與大將阿普·馬雅塔、維卡基勞議事。二將進言:「您年邁勞損,不宜親冒大險。上策是放棄庫斯科,退往奇塔,再據堅城卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納,與昌卡人議和。」庫西·印加·尤潘琪得知父親決意棄城,便直言進諫:「父親!您怎忍心聽從這等可恥的建議,捨棄庫斯科——太陽與維拉科查之城?您取了神的名,神許您與子孫成為大主!」雖是少年,他說話卻如大丈夫般無畏。父親斥他:「你還是個孩子,說話不知輕重,不值一提。」庫西答道:「我願留在讓人們記住的地方。我決不離開庫斯科,決不捨棄太陽之屋!」於是維拉科查攜庶子烏爾庫、索索退往奇塔;庫西留守庫斯科,誓與城共存亡。七位首領與他同守。

sensitivity.note: The defiance that made the king; Sarmiento undercuts it by attributing the scene to Apu Mayta's intrigues.

passages.text: These captains said to him: 'Inca Viracocha!... After careful consideration it appears to us that as you are old and infirm owing to what you have undergone in former wars, it will not be well that you should attempt so great a business, dangerous and with victory doubtful... The wisest counsel respecting the course you should adopt is that you should leave Cuzco, and proceed to the place of Chita, and thence to Caquia Xaquixahuana, which is a strong fort, whence you may treat for an agreement with the Chancas.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when Cusi Inca Yupanqui found that his father was determined to leave Cuzco, they say that he thus addressed him: 'How father can it fit into your heart to accept such infamous advice as to leave Cuzco, city of the Sun and of Viracocha, whose name you have taken, whose promise you hold that you shall be a great lord, you and your descendants.' Though a boy, he said this with the animated daring of a man high in honour. The father answered that he was a boy and that he spoke like one... Inca Yupanqui replied that he would remain where they would be remembered, that he would not leave Cuzco nor abandon the House of the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Viracocha left Cuzco and went to Chita, taking with him his two illegitimate sons Inca Urco and Inca Socso. His son Inca Yupanqui remained at Cuzco, resolved to defend the city or die in its defence. Seven chiefs remained with him: Inca Rocca his elder and legitimate brother, Apu Mayta, Vicaquirau, Quillis-cacha, Urco Huaranca, Chima Chaui Pata Yupanqui, Viracocha Inca Paucar, and Mircoy-mana the tutor of Inca Yupanqui.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 26 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Vision at Susurpuquio: A Mirror Showing the Provinces to Come
title.zh: 蘇蘇爾普基奧顯聖:映出未來疆土的明鏡

region.en: Susurpuquio spring on the road to Xaquixahuana (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 通往夏基夏瓜納路上的蘇蘇爾普基奧泉(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: While this was proceeding with the messengers of the Chancas, the Chanca army was coming nearer to Cuzco. Inca Yupanqui made great praying to Viracocha and to the Sun to protect the city. One day he was at Susurpuquio in great affliction, thinking over the best plan for opposing his enemies, when there appeared a person in the air like the Sun, consoling him and animating him for the battle. This being held up to him a mirror in which the provinces he would subdue were shown, and told him that he would be greater than any of his ancestors: he was to have no doubt, but to return to the city, because he would conquer the Chancas who were marching on Cuzco. With these words the vision animated Inca Yupanqui. He took the mirror, which he carried with him ever afterwards, in peace or war, and returned to the city, where he began to encourage those he had left there.
summary.zh: 昌卡軍日益逼近。印加·尤潘琪向維拉科查與太陽苦苦祈禱,求佑城池。一日,他懷著沉重的憂思來到蘇蘇爾普基奧,盤算退敵之策。忽然,空中現出一人,形貌如太陽,撫慰他、為他壯膽。那神人舉起一面明鏡,鏡中映出他日後將要征服的各省,並說:他必超越歷代先王;叫他勿疑,速回城中——進犯庫斯科的昌卡人必為他所敗。異象之言使印加·尤潘琪勇氣倍增。他取過那面明鏡,從此不離左右——和平時帶著,征戰時也帶著——隨即回城,鼓舞留守軍民。

sensitivity.note: The mirror of conquest - the central legitimation vision of Pachacuti; Molina tells a crystal variant of the same spring episode.

title.en: Chanan-ccuri Coca: The Woman Who Turned the Chanca Assault
title.zh: 查南-庫里-科卡:獨退昌卡攻城的女子

region.zh: 庫斯科喬科斯-查科納坊(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Those who entered by a suburb called Chocos-chacona were valiantly repulsed by the inhabitants. They say that a woman named Chanan-ccuri-coca here fought like a man, and so valiantly opposed the Chancas that they were obliged to retire. This was the cause that all the Chancas who saw it were dismayed.
summary.zh: 自喬科斯-查科納坊突入的昌卡兵,被城中居民奮勇擊退。相傳一位名叫查南-庫里-科卡的女子在此如男子般奮戰,拼死抗擊昌卡人,終使他們被迫退卻。親眼目睹的昌卡人無不喪膽。

sensitivity.note: The named woman defender of Cuzco; a rare female combat hero in the dynastic tradition.

title.en: Men Sent by the Creator: The First Victory and the Name Pachacuti
title.zh: 造物主遣來的神兵:首捷與「帕查庫提」之名

region.en: Cuzco and the hills around (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科及其四郊山嶺(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Inca Yupanqui meanwhile was so quick and dexterous with his weapon that those who carried the statue of Uscovilca became alarmed, and their fear was increased when they saw great numbers of men coming down from the hills. They say that these were sent by Viracocha, the creator, as succour for the Inca. The Chancas began to give way, leaving the statue of Uscovilca, and they say even that of Ancovilca. Attacking on two sides, Inca Rocca, Apu Mayta, and Vicaquirau made great havock among the Chancas. The men of Cuzco continued the pursuit for more than two leagues. The Cuzcos rejoiced at this victory won with so little expectation or hope. They honoured Inca Yupanqui with many epithets, especially calling him PACHACUTI, which means 'over-turner of the earth', alluding to the land and farms which they looked upon as lost by the coming of the Chancas; for he had made them free and safe again. From that time he was called Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪揮器如飛,令扛抬烏斯科維爾卡神像的昌卡人心生恐懼;而當他們望見大群戰士從山上滾滾而下時,恐懼更甚。相傳那些人正是造物主維拉科查為援助印加而遣來的神兵。昌卡軍開始潰退,丟下烏斯科維爾卡的神像——據說連安科維爾卡的神像也丟了。印加·羅卡、阿普·馬雅塔與維卡基勞兩面夾擊,殺得昌卡人屍橫遍野;庫斯科人追擊兩萊格有餘。這場誰也沒想到能贏的大捷令全城歡騰。人們以種種美名尊稱印加·尤潘琪,尤其是「帕查庫提」——意即「翻轉大地者」,指那些因昌卡來犯而被視為必失的土地田園;因為他使它們重獲自由與安寧。自此他便被稱為帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪。

sensitivity.note: The petrified-ally (pururaucas) miracle behind the name Pachacuti; the divine-reinforcement motif of the conquest ideology.

title.en: Treading on the Spoils: A Father's Refusal and a Son's Triumph
title.zh: 踐踏戰利品:父王的推拒與兒子的凱旋

region.zh: 奇塔與卡基亞-夏基夏瓜納(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 27, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As soon as the victory was secure, Inca Yupanqui did not wish to enjoy the triumph. He wished to give his father the glory of such a great victory. So he collected the most precious spoils, and took them to his father who was in Chita, with a principal orejon named Quillis-cachi Urco Huaranca. By him he sent to ask his father to enjoy that triumph and tread on those spoils of the enemy, a custom they have as a sign of victory. When Quillis-cachi Urco Huaranca arrived before Viracocha Inca, he placed those spoils of the Chancas at his feet with great reverence, saying: 'Inca Viracocha! thy son Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui, to whom the Sun has given such a great victory... sends me to salute you, and says that, as a good and humble son he wishes you to triumph over your victory and to tread upon these spoils of your enemies.' Inca Viracocha did not wish to tread on them, but said that his son Inca Urco should do so, as he was to succeed to the Incaship. Hearing this the messenger rose and gave utterance to furious words, saying that he did not come for cowards to triumph by the deeds of Pachacuti. He added that if Viracocha did not wish to receive this recognition from so valiant a son, it would be better that Pachacuti should enjoy the glory for which he had worked. With this he returned to Cuzco, and told Pachacuti what had happened with his father.
summary.zh: 大捷甫定,印加·尤潘琪不願獨享凱旋,欲將榮光歸於父親。他收集最珍貴的戰利品,由重臣基利斯-卡奇·烏爾科·瓦蘭卡押送至奇塔父王行轅,請父王踐踏敵酋遺物、共享凱旋——這是他們表示勝利的禮制。使者到後,恭恭敬敬將昌卡戰利品置於維拉科查足前:「印加·維拉科查!您的兒子帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪——太陽賜予他如此大捷——命我前來問安。他願以孝順謙卑之子之身,請父親享受凱旋,踐踏敵人的戰利品。」維拉科查卻不肯踐踏,說應由儲君印加·烏爾庫代行。使者聞言霍然起身,憤然說道:「我可不是來讓懦夫借帕查庫提的功勞沾光的!您若不肯受這樣勇武之子的尊崇,那便請帕查庫提自己享用他拚來的榮耀吧!」言畢返回庫斯科,將父親的態度告訴了帕查庫提。

sensitivity.note: The triumph ritual (treading the spoils) turned into a legitimacy contest between father and son.

title.en: Child of the Sun, Guardian of Cuzco: The Reply and the Hatchet
title.zh: 太陽之子、庫斯科守護者:答書與戰斧

region.en: Ichu-pampa, five leagues west of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以西五萊格的伊丘-潘帕(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 28, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As soon as the two forces came in sight of each other, Asto-huaraca, full of arrogance, sent to Inca Yupanqui to tell him that they were not like him coming from the poverty stricken Cuzco, and that unless he repented the past and became a tributary and vassal to the Chancas, Asto-huaraca would dye his lance in an Inca's blood. But Inca Yupanqui was not terrified by the embassy. He answered: 'Go back, brother, and say to Asto-huaraca, your Sinchi, that Inca Yupanqui is a child of the Sun and guardian of Cuzco, the city of Ticci Viracocha Pachayachachi, by whose order I am here guarding it. For this city is not mine but his; and if your Sinchi should wish to own obedience to Ticci Viracocha, or to me in His name, he will be honourably received. If your Sinchi should see things in another light, show him that I am here with our friends, and if he should conquer us he can call himself Lord and Inca. But let him understand that no more time can be wasted in demands and replies. God (Ticci Viracocha) will give the victory to whom he pleases.' The two armies approached each other in Ichu-pampa, encountered, and mixed together... At last Pachacuti made a way to where Asto-huaraca was fighting, attacked him and delivered a blow with his hatchet which cut off the Chanca's head. Tomay-huaraca was already killed. The Inca caused the heads of these two captains to be set on the points of lances, and raised on high to be seen by their followers. The Chancas, on seeing the heads, despaired of victory without leaders.
summary.zh: 兩軍望見彼此时,驕横的阿斯托-瓦拉卡遣使羞辱印加·尤潘琪:你們不過來自窮困的庫斯科;若不悔過稱臣,他的長矛必染印加之血。印加·尤潘琪絲毫不為所動,答曰:「回去告訴你們的辛奇阿斯托-瓦拉卡:印加·尤潘琪是太陽之子、庫斯科的守護者——庫斯科乃提基·維拉科查·帕查亞查奇之城,奉其命我守衛於此。此城非我所有,乃神之城。你們的辛奇若願向提基·維拉科查——或以神之名向我——俯首,必受禮遇。若他執迷不悟,那就叫他看著:我與我的朋友們在此;他若能勝我,自可稱主稱王。但叫他明白:索貢與回文,到此為止。勝利屬於誰,提基·維拉科查自會定奪。」兩軍在伊丘-潘帕相撞混戰。終於,帕查庫提殺開血路,直取阿斯托-瓦拉卡,一斧揮落其頭顱;托馬伊-瓦拉卡已先被擊斃。印加王命將二酋首級懸於長矛頂端,高高舉起示眾。昌卡人見酋首,自度無主必敗,潰散而逃。

sensitivity.note: The war-embassy exchange formulates Inca conquest theology in one sentence: the city belongs to Viracocha.

passages.text: Asto-huaraca, full of arrogance, sent to Inca Yupanqui to tell him that he could see the power of the Chancas and the position they now held. They were not like him coming from the poverty stricken Cuzco, and if he did not repent the past and become a tributary and vassal to the Chancas; Asto-huaraca would dye his lance in an Inca's blood. But Inca Yupanqui was not terrified by the embassy. He answered in this way to the messenger: 'Go back brother and say to Asto-huaraca, your Sinchi, that Inca Yupanqui is a child of the Sun and guardian of Cuzco, the city of Ticci Viracocha Pachayachachi, by whose order I am here guarding it. For this city is not mine but his; and if your Sinchi should wish to own obedience to Ticci Viracocha, or to me in His name, he will be honourably received... But let him understand that no more time can be wasted in demands and replies. God (Ticci Viracocha) will give the victory to whom he pleases.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 28 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Pachacuti made a way to where Asto-huaraca was fighting, attacked him and delivered a blow with his hatchet which cut off the Chanca's head. Tomay-huaraca was already killed. The Inca caused the heads of these two captains to be set on the points of lances, and raised on high to be seen by their followers. The Chancas, on seeing the heads, despaired of victory without leaders. They gave up the contest and sought safety in flight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 28 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Fringe Found on the Image: How the Sun's Oracle Crowned Pachacuti
title.zh: 神像自戴王纓:太陽神諭為帕查庫提加冕

region.en: Inti-cancha, House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋因蒂-坎恰(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 29, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: When the Inca Yupanqui found himself so strong and that he had been joined by so many people, he determined not to wait for the nomination of his father, much less for his death. With this object he caused a grand sacrifice to be offered to the Sun in the Inti-cancha or House of the Sun, and then went to ask the image of the Sun who should be Inca. The oracle of the devil, or perhaps some Indian who was behind to give the answer, replied that Inca Yupanqui Pachacuti was chosen and should be Inca. On this answer being given, all who were present at the sacrifice prostrated themselves before Pachacuti, crying out 'Ccapac Inca Intip Churin' - Sovereign Lord Child of the Sun. Presently they prepared a very rich fringe of gold and emeralds wherewith to crown him. Next day they took Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui to the House of the Sun, and when they came to the image of the Sun, which was of gold and the size of a man, they found it with the fringe, as if offering it of its own will. First making his sacrifices, according to their custom, he came to the image, and the High Priest called out in his language 'Intip Apu' - Governor of things pertaining to the Sun. With much ceremony and great reverence the fringe was taken from the image and placed, with much pomp, on the forehead of Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui. Then all called his name and hailed him 'Intip Churin Inca Pachacuti' - Child of the Sun Lord, over-turner of the earth.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪羽翼已豐,歸附者日眾,遂決意不再等候父親的冊立——更不必等他壽終。他在太陽之屋向太陽隆重獻祭,然後叩問太陽神像:誰當為印加王?神諭——薩爾米恩托說是「魔鬼的神諭,或許只是躲在像後傳話的某個印第安人」——答道:帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪已被選中,當為印加王。此言一出,與祭眾人皆拜倒於帕查庫提之前,高呼「卡帕克·印加·因蒂普·丘林」——太陽之子、至尊之主。眾人隨即製備鑲祖母綠的華美金王纓。次日,眾人擁帕查庫提至太陽之屋;行至金鑄的、如真人大小太陽神像前,卻見王纓已掛在神像之上——彷彿神像自願奉出。他依俗獻祭完畢,走近神像;大祭司以土語高呼「因蒂普·阿普」——司太陽之事之主。於是,在極隆重的儀式中,王纓自神像取下,莊嚴地繫於帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪的額前。眾人齊呼其號:「因蒂普·丘林·印加·帕查庫提」——太陽之主的兒子,翻轉大地者。

sensitivity.note: The self-offering oracle fringe; Sarmiento's aside ('or perhaps some Indian who was behind') is preserved as part of the record - a rare colonial demystification embedded in the myth.

title.en: The Sun Watches Through the Pillars: Sucanca and Inti-huatana
title.zh: 陽光穿柱:蘇坎卡與拴日石

region.zh: 庫斯科以東山丘(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 30, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: In order that the precise time of sowing and harvesting might be known, and that nothing might be lost, the Inca caused four poles to be set up on a high mountain to the east of Cuzco, about two varas apart, on the heads of which there were holes, by which the sun entered, in the manner of a watch or astrolabe. Observing where the sun struck the ground through these holes, at the time of sowing and harvest, marks were made on the ground. Other poles were set up in the part corresponding to the west of Cuzco, for the time of harvesting the maize. Having fixed the positions exactly by these poles, they built columns of stone for perpetuity in their places, of the height of the poles and with holes in like places. All round it was ordered that the ground should be paved; and on the stones certain lines were drawn, conforming to the movements of the sun entering through the holes in the columns. Thus the whole became an instrument serving for an annual time-piece, by which the times of sowing and harvesting were regulated. Persons were appointed to observe these watches, and to notify to the people the times they indicated. Markham's note identifies the pillars as the Sucanca - the two pillars denoting the beginning of winter, whence the year was measured, were called Pucuy Sucanca; those notifying the beginning of spring were Chirao Sucanca - and the equinox column before the temple of the Sun as the Inti-huatana, the 'sun-seizer', where a line was drawn from east to west and they watched when the shadow of the pillar was on the line and there was no shadow at noon.
summary.zh: 為使播種收穫各得其時、寸陰不廢,印加王命人在庫斯科以東的高山上豎立四根木柱,間距約兩瓦拉,柱頭鑿孔,讓陽光穿孔而入——一如日晷或星盤。播種與收穫之時,觀察日光穿孔投於地面的位置,在地面做下記號。庫斯科以西相應之處也豎立木柱,以定收玉米之期。位置定準之後,便在原處砌起石柱,以垂永久——石柱與木柱同高,孔位相同;柱基四周鋪石,石面刻線,與陽光穿孔的移動軌跡相合。整座裝置遂成為一座年度報時儀,用以規定播種與收穫之期;又設專人值守觀測,向民眾宣告時令。據馬卡姆注,這些石柱稱「蘇坎卡」:標誌冬季開始(即歲首)的兩柱稱「普庫伊·蘇坎卡」,標誌春季開始的稱「奇勞·蘇坎卡」;而太陽神廟前空地中央立於大圓圈內的石柱,則是「因蒂-瓦塔納」——「拴日石」:自東至西畫一條線,日出至日落間柱影落在線上而正午無影之時,便是春分秋分。

sensitivity.note: Astronomical pillars as calendrical ritual technology; the 'sun-seized' etymology of Inti-huatana is Markham's.

passages.text: In order that the precise time of sowing and harvesting might be known, and that nothing might be lost, the Inca caused four poles to be set up on a high mountain to the east of Cuzco, about two varas apart, on the heads of which there were holes, by which the sun entered, in the manner of a watch or astrolabe. Observing where the sun struck the ground through these holes, at the time of sowing and harvest, marks were made on the ground... Having fixed the positions exactly by these poles, they built columns of stone for perpetuity in their places... Thus the whole became an instrument serving for an annual time-piece, by which the times of sowing and harvesting were regulated. Persons were appointed to observe these watches, and to notify to the people the times they indicated.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 30 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The pillars at Cuzco to determine the time of the solstices were called Sucanca. The two pillars denoting the beginning of winter, whence the year was measured, were called Pucuy Sucanca. Those notifying the beginning of spring were Chirao Sucanca... To ascertain the time of the equinoxes there was a stone column in the open space before the temple of the Sun in the centre of a large circle. This was the Inti-huatana. A line was drawn across from east to west and they watched when the shadow of the pillar was on the line from sunrise to sunset and there was no shadow at noon.
passages.note: Markham's note condensed (Hakluyt Society 1907); reported as editorial annotation to Sarmiento's text.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: Golden Doors on the Window: Pachacuti Honours the Cave of Origins
title.zh: 金門封窗:帕查庫提朝拜始祖之洞

region.zh: 坦波-托科(帕卡里坦波)(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 30, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: As he was curious about the things of antiquity, and wished to perpetuate his name, the Inca went personally to the hill of Tampu-tocco or Paccari-tampu - names for the same thing - and entered the cave whence it is held for certain that Manco Ccapac and his brethren came when they marched to Cuzco for the first time. After he had made a thorough inspection, he venerated the locality and showed his feeling by festivals and sacrifices. He placed doors of gold on the window Ccapac-tocco, and ordered that from that time forward the locality should be venerated by all, making it a prayer place and huaca, whither to go to pray for oracles and to sacrifice.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提酷好古事,又欲名垂不朽,便親往坦波-托科(即帕卡里坦波,同名異稱)之山,鑽進那傳說中曼科·卡帕克與兄弟們首次出征庫斯科時所出的洞穴。他仔細察看之後,對聖地行禮致敬,以節慶與祭祀表達敬意;又命人在卡帕克-托科之窗安上黃金之門,下令從此全民崇敬此處,奉為祈禱之所與瓦卡——人們可到那裡求取神諭、舉行獻祭。

sensitivity.note: The dynasty's birthplace shrine refurbished by its greatest restorer; gold doors on the emergence window.
